newsitem.title: USA: NYS hits 100-day in budget talks, still battling.
newsitem.headline: NYS hits 100-day in budget talks, still battling.

text.p: New York State on Wednesday hit the 100th day in budget talks, but Gov. George Pataki made it clear that battles over controversial issues, from welfare to tax reform to new prisons, still were being fought.

Asked if his Administration was narrowing differences over the issues, he told reporters in Albany: "Some issues are getting closer, some issues are not. It's very difficult because we're really talking about dramatic changes."

New York State Controller H. Carl McCall, in prepared remarks, faulted Pataki for a lack of leadership. "A well-written term paper handed in four months after the end of the semester is still given a failing grade, and a budget that is 100 days late is a failed budget, no matter how good the final product."

Pataki did not say whether he would accept less than 7,000 new prison cells, saying only that while he always was willing to listen to arguments, he was going to make sure violent felons were not released due to a lack of space.

The Democrat-led Assembly wants a smaller program--800 new maximum security cells plus 800 new drug treatment beds, calling the governor's proposal, which would be paid for with $650 million of new revenue bonds, a jobs program for upstate New York. The area, a Republican stronghold, was considered likely to ask that any new prisons be built there.
The New York Times, in its Wednesday edition, said Pataki had backed down from at least part of his welfare plan, which would have reduced cash benefits to families over five years.

The paper, citing anonymous officials in the legislature and the governor's office, added Pataki was expected to scale back a voucher program that would replace the state Home Relief plan for childless, able-bodied adults, by offering both vouchers and cash aid.
The Disability Coalition, a group of 25 organizations that serve poor and disabled New Yorkers, called on Pataki to approve laws the Assembly's agreed in its welfare program.

The group, in a prepared statement, said the Republican governor still wanted a time limit on benefits for the disabled, was fighting for a narrow definition of disability, instead of a broader one under the Americans with Disabilities Act, and was still pushing for the right to assign disabled workers to worfare programs against their doctors' orders. The issue is a controversial one due to the death of a disabled New York City woman who participated in a workfare program.

Pataki said the disabilities act was aimed at encouraging individuals who were physically able to do so to work, adding "There are serious efforts to derail our necessary movement of people from welfare to workfare and we're going to continue to push on that." He criticized Assembly leaders for wanting to use the Americans with Disabilities Act standard.
Pataki added the Assembly, which fought to protect rent rules, had inserted a clause in the new laws letting landlords raise leases for vacant apartment by as much as 29 percent.

New York State Tenants and Neighbors Coalition, which battled to keep rent rules from expiring, said nine percent of that rise was unlawful and called on Pataki to rescind a housing official's memo it said encourages landlords to assess the extra increase.
